ch07.note: Rehe (热河), or Jehol, a former province of the mountainous borderland north-east of Beiping. In February–March 1933 the Japanese Kwantung Army overran it in a swift campaign (the “Operation Nekka”), annexing it to the puppet state of Manchukuo and carrying the fighting down to the passes of the Great Wall; the province was abolished in 1955.

Cai E (蔡锷, 1882–1916), the Yunnan general who in 1915 slipped out of Yuan Shikai’s Beijing—by popular legend with the help of the sing-song girl Xiao Fengxian (小凤仙), whose favours gave him his cover—to raise the National Protection War against Yuan’s attempt to make himself emperor. Their romance became a stock subject of opera, stage, and screen, which is the “Xiao Fengxian” Chen means.

The 八大胡同, a cluster of lanes just south of Qianmen that formed Beiping’s licensed pleasure quarter. The first-class houses advertised themselves as “pure-singing houses” (清吟小班), where in principle the women sold their song and their company rather than their bodies; 平康里 (Pingkangli) is a classical literary name for such a district.

打茶围, the custom of a paid introductory visit to a courtesan: the guest sits with her over tea, melon seeds, cigarettes, and talk, appraising her while she appraises his purse. It carried a set fee and, at a proper “home” room, formally opened the acquaintance; it implied nothing further of itself.
Zhang Zongchang (张宗昌, 1881–1932), warlord of Shandong, nicknamed the “Dog-Meat General,” a byword for brute cruelty, uncounted concubines, and buffoonery; driven out in 1928 and assassinated in 1932.

Manchukuo (满洲国), the puppet state Japan set up in the Northeast in 1932 under the last Qing emperor, Puyi. The Japanese aim Chen describes was to engineer a comparable client regime across North China—the project the Zhang Jingyao affair was part of.

ch07.anchor: The Secret Records of President Chiang
ch07.note: 蒋总统秘录, a documentary biography of Chiang Kai-shek drawn largely from Nationalist archives, serialized in Japan’s Sankei Shimbun in the mid-1970s and issued in Chinese translation by the Central Daily News (中央日报) in Taipei. Chen quotes the Chinese edition.

Duan Qirui (段祺瑞, 1865–1936), the Beiyang premier and head of the Anhui clique who dominated the Beijing government in the late 1910s; by 1933 long out of power and living in retirement, which is why the Japanese hoped to draw him out.

Song Zheyuan (宋哲元, 1885–1940), commander of the Twenty-Ninth Army in North China; his troops fought the Japanese at the Great Wall passes in 1933 and again at the Marco Polo Bridge in July 1937. Zhang Jingyao’s claim of “deep ties” to him, on which Itagaki paid out, appears to have been a boast.

ch07.anchor: A Tale of Heroic Sons and Daughters
ch07.note: 儿女英雄传, a mid-nineteenth-century novel by Wen Kang. Its heroine, Shisanmei (十三妹, “Thirteenth Sister”) He Yufeng, sets out to avenge her murdered father but is dissuaded before she can strike—hence Chen’s point that Shi Jianqiao, who did carry her revenge through, went a step further.

The Xinchou Treaty (辛丑条约) of 1901, imposed on the Qing by the eight allied powers after the Boxer Uprising. It fixed a vast indemnity and formalized the Legation Quarter as a walled, foreign-garrisoned enclave into which Chinese authority could not reach—the “humiliating brand” Chen names.
